newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka's Jayewardene dies, leaves mixed legacy.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka's Jayewardene dies, leaves mixed legacy.

text.p: Former Sri Lankan President Junius Richard Jayewardene died on Friday, ending a political life that saw his country move from hope after independence from Britain in 1948 to the tragedy of a bitter ethnic war.

Jayewardene, 90, who led the Indian Ocean island for 11 years from 1977 to 1988 as prime minister and executive president, died of heart failure at a private hospital in Colombo where he was being treated for cancer, hospital officials said.

Jayewardene was credited with liberalising a rigid socialist economy but criticised for authoritarianism and for failing to stem a bloody war with Tamils fighting for an independent state in northern and eastern Sri Lanka.
Nicknamed "the old fox" for his political shrewdness, Jayewardene survived four assassination attempts during his long public career.
"He showed Sri Lanka the path to the new world," said Ranil Wickremesinghe, head of the United National Party, the retired Jayewardene's political group.
"He set us on the path to modernisation, a path which has been followed by successive governments," Wickremesinghe, a former prime minister, told a news conference.

Analysts said the late leader's ultimate legacy is the war, which began on his watch in 1983 and rages on today, having caused immeasurable damage to the economy and cost at least 50,000 lives while creating about 500,000 refugees.

Jayewardene will be irrevocably associated with a controversial pact with India in 1987 aimed at ending the war by Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) guerrillas for independence for minority Tamils in the north and east.
The accord led to the arrival of tens of thousands of Indian troops on the island in a bloody but unsuccessful bid to disarm the Tamil separatists.
Jayewardene won a landslide victory in a 1977 general election which gave his United National Party (UNP) an unprecedented four-fifths majority in parliament.
The next year he changed the British-style parliamentary system to an executive presidency and assumed the post of president with sweeping powers.
Scrapping statist economic policies, Jayewardene dismantled import and foreign exchange controls, opening the economy with the words "let the robber barons come in".
In 1982 he called a presidential election 16 months early and was re-elected.

But, anxious to retain his steam-roller majority in parliament, Jayewardene held a controversial referendum the same year to extend parliament by a further six years without a general election, despite protests from the opposition.
Political analysts said this fuelled the rise of the 1988-90 Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (People's Liberation Front) leftwing insurgency, which claimed thousands of lives.
Jayewardene represented Ceylon at the Japanese Peace Treaty Conference at San Fransisco in 1951 to decide the fate of Japan and the question of reparations.
The son of a former chief justice, Jayewardene was born on September 17, 1906 and started as a lawyer before entering politics as a member of the Colombo Municipal Council in 1940.
Jayewardene survived four assassination attempts during his 50 years in politics, the last being in 1987 when two hand grenades were lobbed at a ruling UNP meeting in parliament by a JVP activist.

One of the grenades fell on the table at which Jayewardene was sitting and rolled off before exploding.Two people were killed and five ministers were wounded but Jayewardene, a devout Buddhist, escaped without a scratch.
